1.open: Who is someone you admire so much that you would happily listen to them talk for an hour, and what is it about them?
questions: Paul writes to the church "sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy" (v. 2), and then spends the chapter correcting them. What does it tell you that he starts by calling them holy?

Paul thanks God for the grace given to the Corinthians before he says anything hard (vv. 4 to 7). Why might he begin there, and how could we do the same when we need to talk to someone about a problem?
Some in the church said, "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," or "I follow Cephas" (v. 12). What are the modern versions of this, such as favorite pastors, authors, podcasts, or church styles?
Paul asks, "Is Christ divided?" (v. 13). What does that question suggest about how God sees a church that splits into camps?

Verse 18 says "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." When have you found the cross hard to make sense of, or hard to explain to someone else? Be as honest as you like.
Paul says "the foolishness of God is wiser than man's wisdom" (v. 25). Where have you seen something that looked weak or foolish turn out to matter more than something strong or clever?
Paul tells them, "Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth" (v. 26). How does it feel to hear that God chose people like this on purpose?
The chapter ends with "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord" (v. 31). What do you tend to take pride in, and what would it look like to point that credit back to God?
1.life: Think of one person or group in your church or community you tend to see as on the other side, or one leader you lean on more than you lean on Christ. This week, say something kind about them to someone else, or tell them thank you.
1.prayer: Thank God that he calls ordinary, flawed people his holy ones. Ask him to heal any divisions among us and to keep the cross at the center of everything we do.
1.tip: The "foolishness" language in verses 18 to 25 can be heard as an attack on education or thinking. Gently point out that Paul is not against learning. He is saying that no amount of cleverness is how anyone finds God, and that pride in being smart or impressive is the real problem.

2.open: Think of the best speaker or storyteller you have ever heard. What made them so good to listen to?
questions: Paul says he "resolved to know nothing" among them "except Jesus Christ and Him crucified" (v. 2). Why might a crucified Savior have been an awkward thing to talk about in Paul's day, and in ours?
Paul admits he came "in weakness and fear, and with much trembling" (v. 3). How does it land for you that he was honest about being nervous?

Paul wanted their faith to rest on God's power and not on human wisdom (v. 5). What do people lean on today to feel sure about what they believe: a good speaker, a big crowd, a strong argument, a feeling?
Verse 9 says no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined "what God has prepared for those who love Him." What do you picture when you hear that, and what do you find hard to picture?
Paul says "no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God" (v. 11). How does his comparison to our own inner thoughts help you understand what the Spirit does?
Verse 14 says that to the natural man these things are "foolishness." Have you ever found the message of Jesus strange or hard to accept? Be as honest as you like, including about right now.
Paul ends with "we have the mind of Christ" (v. 16). What would it look like for that to shape how you handle one ordinary part of your week?

Some Christians read "the mature" and "the spiritual" as a special group of advanced believers, and others read them as anyone who has received God's Spirit. How does each reading change the way you hear this chapter?
2.life: This week, when you are tempted to win an argument or impress someone, pause and ask God for his help instead. Then pick one person and simply share something Jesus has done for you, in plain words and without polish.
2.prayer: Thank God that his Spirit helps us understand what we could never work out alone. Ask for humility to rely on God's power, and for honest openness about where faith still feels hard.
2.tip: Verses 14 and 15 can sound like believers are smarter or better than everyone else, which will sting anyone in the room who is doubting. Say plainly that Paul is talking about the Spirit's help, not about intelligence or status, and that the chapter leaves no room for pride. Mention the disagreement over "the mature" briefly and move on.

3.open: Who is a teacher, coach or mentor who helped you grow, and what did they do that made the difference?
questions: Paul says he gave them "milk, not solid food" (v. 2). What do you think the milk and the solid food stand for, and how can you tell when someone is ready for more?
The Corinthians were saying "I follow Paul" and "I follow Apollos" (v. 4). Why do people line up behind a favorite speaker, author or church? What do they gain, and what might they lose?
Paul says, "I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow" (v. 6). Who planted or watered your faith, and what does it mean that God was the one making it grow?
In verse 7 Paul says "neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God." How could that free a leader from pressure? How could it free the rest of us from comparing?
Verse 11 says the foundation is "Jesus Christ." What are some things people build on top of that foundation, and how can we tell whether they are gold or straw?

Verse 15 says a builder whose work burns up "will suffer loss. He himself will be saved." Christians read the fire in verses 13 to 15 differently, and some link it to purgatory. What do you take from the picture that someone can be saved and still lose something?
Paul says "you yourselves are God's temple" (v. 16), and the word "you" is plural. What changes if God's presence is with the whole community and not only with each of us alone?
Paul ends with "you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God" (v. 23). If you are not sure that feels true for you right now, what makes it hard to believe, and what would help?
3.life: This week, thank one person who planted or watered your faith, by note, text or in person. Then notice one moment when you compare yourself to another believer, and hand it over to God, who makes things grow.
3.prayer: Thank God for the people who helped your faith grow, and for the God who "makes things grow." Ask for humility, for unity in your group, and for a desire to build with lasting materials.
3.tip: Verses 13 to 15 can pull the group into a debate about judgment and purgatory. Name in one line that Christians read the fire differently, then steer back to the main point: Christ is the foundation, and the church is one body, not rival camps.

4.open: Who is someone you admire, and what is it about them that makes you look up to them?
questions: Paul says leaders should be seen as "servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God" (v. 1). What do you think it means to be trusted with something that belongs to someone else?
Verse 2 says "it is required of stewards that they be found faithful." Notice it does not say successful or impressive. What does faithful look like in ordinary life, at home, at work or in church?
Paul says, "I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court" (v. 3). Whose opinion do you find hardest to ignore, and why?
Verse 5 says the Lord "will expose the motives of men’s hearts." Does that feel more like a relief or a worry to you right now? Be as honest as you like.
Paul asks, "What do you have that you did not receive?" (v. 7). Think of a skill, an opportunity or a person in your life. How would it change things to see it as a gift?

In verses 8 to 13 Paul says the Corinthians feel like kings while the apostles are hungry, poorly clothed and treated as "the scum of the earth" (v. 13). Why might comfort and success make it harder to see what following Jesus costs?

Paul says, "I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children" (v. 14). How can you tell the difference between correction that comes from love and correction that only wants to put you down?
Verse 20 says "the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power." Where have you seen faith show up in a life, not just in words?
4.life: This week, pick one person you tend to rank above or below yourself, whether a leader, a coworker or a relative. Each time you catch yourself judging them, thank God for something good in them and leave the rest to him.
4.prayer: Thank God that every good thing you have is a gift. Ask him to help you be faithful in small things, and to free you from needing everyone's approval.
4.tip: Verse 5 can be heard as a warning that makes anxious people feel worse. Point out that Paul ends it with "each will receive his praise from God," and let anyone who is unsure how they feel about being fully known speak honestly. Also keep the group from using verses 3 to 5 to dodge all accountability; Paul is talking about proud ranking of leaders, not about never speaking into each other's lives.

5.open: Think of a group you have belonged to, like a team, a family or a club. What is one unwritten rule that everyone there just knew?
questions: Paul says the church was "proud" when they should have been "stricken with grief" (v. 2). Why might a church feel proud about something like this? What would grief have looked like instead?
Paul wants the church to act together "in the name of our Lord Jesus" (v. 4). Why do you think he insists this be a shared decision and not something one person handles quietly?
Paul says the aim is "so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord" (v. 5). How does that change the way you read the instruction to put the man out?
Paul asks, "Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" (v. 6). Where have you seen one unaddressed problem change the feel of a whole group?
Paul says, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (v. 7). How does what Jesus has already done shape the way we are asked to live together?
Paul separates people who claim to be believers from "the sexually immoral of this world" (v. 10). Why does he draw that line? What would go wrong if the church tried to police everyone outside it?
The list in verse 11 includes the greedy, the "verbal abuser" and the "drunkard" beside sexual immorality. Which of these is easiest for churches to overlook, and why?
Be honest: what do you find hard or uncomfortable about this chapter? Where would you want to hear more before you feel settled about it?
5.life: Think of one person in your life who has drifted from the group or from faith, or who is carrying something heavy. This week, reach out with a simple invitation, like a coffee or a call, and listen more than you talk.
5.prayer: Thank God that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed for us. Ask for honesty about our own lives, and for wisdom and gentleness toward anyone who has gone astray.
5.tip: Christians disagree about what handing the man over to Satan means and about how strictly churches today should remove members. Say so plainly, then keep the group on Paul's stated hope for the man's salvation and on the question of how your own group shows honesty and care. Be ready for someone in the room who has been hurt by church discipline, and let them speak without rushing to defend or correct.

6.open: What is something you own that you would be upset to see someone treat carelessly?
questions: Paul is shocked that believers take each other to court "before the unrighteous" (v. 1). Why do you think he cares so much about how Christians handle conflict in front of outsiders?
He asks, "Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?" (v. 7). When have you had to choose between standing up for yourself and letting something go? What did it cost you?

Christians differ on whether verses 1 to 8 forbid believers from ever suing one another in public courts, or mainly rebuke petty lawsuits and cheating while leaving room for the courts in serious wrongs. Where do you find yourself leaning, and why?

Verses 9 and 10 list many ways of living, from greed and drunkenness to sexual sin, that have no share in God's kingdom. Why might Paul put such different things side by side? Which ones do people tend to excuse?

In verse 11 Paul says, "that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified." What does it mean to you that the church in Corinth was made of people with a past? How does that shape the way we welcome people?

Paul says, "Everything is permissible for me," but not everything is beneficial, and "I will not be mastered by anything" (v. 12). What is something good or harmless that can quietly start running your life?

Paul says, "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit" and "You are not your own; you were bought at a price" (vv. 19, 20). When you hear that, do you feel comforted, challenged, or something else? Be as honest as you like, including if it doesn't sit easily with you.
Paul argues that the body matters because God "will raise us also" (v. 14). How might believing your body matters to God change the way you treat it, such as rest, food, screens or relationships?
6.life: Pick one habit or appetite that has more hold on you than you would like. This week, bring it to God honestly each day, and if it helps, tell one trusted person about it. Remember that Paul says you were "washed" first, before any change (v. 11).
6.prayer: Thank God that you are washed, set apart and made right with him by Jesus and the Spirit. Ask for grace to settle conflicts humbly and to care for your body as his.
6.tip: Verses 9 and 10 can make people feel shut out, and two rare words in verse 9 are translated very differently. Most churches read them as ruling out sex between men, while some scholars think Paul meant specific exploitative practices of his day. Say that plainly, don't try to settle it tonight, and bring the group back to verse 11, where Paul's point is what Jesus has done for people with a past.

7.open: What is one big life decision, like a move, a job or a school, that you took longer to make than you expected?
questions: Paul says husband and wife each have a claim on the other, and that they should not "deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time" (vv. 4-5). What does mutual care and consent look like in a marriage? Why does it matter that it goes both ways?
Paul says "each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that" (v. 7). How have you seen singleness or marriage be a good gift, and how have you seen either one be hard?

In verses 10 and 11 Paul passes on a teaching he credits to the Lord about divorce, and in verse 12 he says "I, not the Lord." Why might Paul be so careful to separate the two? Many churches also teach that no one has to stay where they are unsafe. How should that shape the way we read this passage?

Verse 15 says that if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer "is not bound in such cases," and that "God has called you to live in peace." What do you think peace looks like for someone in a hard marriage or a painful divorce?
Paul says, "each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him" (v. 17). Where are you tempted to think your faith would be easier if only your situation were different?
Paul says "you were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men" (v. 23). Where do you feel pressure to please people, or to fit a picture of what your life should look like by now?

Paul says he wants you "to be free from concern" and to have "undivided devotion to the Lord" (vv. 32, 35). Whatever your situation, what pulls your attention away from God most? What helps you come back?
If you are honest, what part of this chapter is hard for you to accept, or leaves you with questions? What would you want to ask Paul?
7.life: Pick one part of your life you keep wishing were different, whether single, married, a job or a season. This week, ask God what faithful living looks like right where you are, and do one small thing about it.
7.prayer: Thank God that he calls people to live faithfully in every season and situation. Pray for anyone in the group who is lonely, waiting, struggling in a marriage, or carrying a hard decision.
7.tip: Divorce and singleness are personal, and someone in the room may be living through a painful version of both. Do not debate the rules. Remind the group that Paul gives some of this as his own judgment, say plainly that Christians differ on how lasting his preference for singleness is, and invite people to share only what they want to. If someone mentions abuse, listen with care and encourage them to talk with a pastor or trusted counselor after the meeting.

8.open: What is something you feel completely free to do that a friend or family member is more careful about?
questions: Paul says, "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (v. 1). When have you seen someone use what they know in a way that made others feel small? When have you seen it done with love?
Verse 2 says the one who thinks he knows something "does not yet know as he ought to know." Where do you find it easy to feel certain, and what might you still be learning?
Verse 3 says "the one who loves God is known by God." Why do you think Paul puts being known by God ahead of knowing things about God?

In Corinth, meat from temple sacrifices was eaten at feasts and sold in the market. Paul agrees that "an idol is nothing at all in the world" (v. 4). Why might he start by agreeing with the confident believers before he challenges them?

Verse 7 describes people who were "still so accustomed to idols" that eating the food troubled their conscience. What habits, places or things from someone's past might still be hard for them today, even if others see no problem?

Paul says, "Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak" (v. 9). What does it look like to give up something you are free to do for the sake of another person, and what might it cost you?

Christians differ on how far this applies, especially on who counts as the weak and how much one person's freedom should give way to another's discomfort. How would you decide where the line is in your own life?
Paul calls the weaker believer someone "for whom Christ died" (v. 11). How does that change the way you think about people whose convictions seem too strict, too loose, or just different from yours?
8.life: Think of one person whose conscience is more sensitive than yours on some question. This week, ask them a real question about it and listen without trying to correct them. If it would help them, adjust one habit around them.
8.prayer: Ask God to make you a person whose knowledge is held with love. Pray for the humility to learn, and for eyes to see the people your choices touch.
8.tip: The group may start debating which modern habits count as 'meat offered to idols,' such as drinking, entertainment or politics. Let people share, but steer back to Paul's question: how does my freedom affect the person next to me? Remind everyone that Christians land in different places, and that the aim is love, not winning.

9.open: What is something you have given up, or gone without, so that someone else could have it better?
questions: Paul begins with questions about his freedom and his standing: "Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?" (v. 1). Why do you think he felt he had to defend himself to the Corinthians?
Paul calls the Corinthian believers "the seal of my apostleship in the Lord" (v. 2). When you look at your own life, whose faith or kindness has been like proof to you that God is real?
In verses 7 to 10, Paul points to soldiers, farmers, shepherds and even an ox. What is the common idea in these pictures, and why would that matter to a church deciding how to treat its leaders?

Paul says the Lord taught that "those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel" (v. 14), yet he chose not to use that right. Why would someone turn down something they are fully owed?

In verse 12 Paul says he would "put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ." What is one thing today that can get in the way of people hearing about Jesus, even when it is not wrong in itself?
Paul writes, "I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible" (v. 19). What is the difference between caring enough to meet people where they are and simply going along with the crowd?
Paul compares his life to training for a race, saying "I do not run aimlessly" (v. 26). Where does your own faith feel aimless or worn out right now, and what would an honest next step look like?
Paul worries about being "disqualified" himself (v. 27). If that verse stirs up fear or doubt for you, what do you want to say about it? What would you like to hear from this group?
9.life: Pick one right, preference or comfort you normally hold on to, such as your time, your opinion or your schedule. This week, set it aside for one person's sake, quietly and without telling anyone why.
9.prayer: Thank God that the good news is given freely. Ask for a generous heart that puts other people first, and for steady, daily discipline in following Jesus.
9.tip: Verse 27 troubles some people, who wonder if Paul is saying a believer can lose salvation. Say plainly that Christians read this differently, and keep the group on Paul's main point: he lives with purpose and does not take his calling lightly. Also be careful that verses 4 to 14 are not used to pressure people about giving to pastors; the chapter's focus is Paul's choice, not a rule for anyone else.

10.open: What is something you are allowed to do but sometimes choose not to, because of the people around you?
questions: Paul reminds the church of Israel's cloud, sea crossing, bread from heaven and water from the rock, yet says "God was not pleased with most of them" (v. 5). What does it tell us that people with so many gifts from God still fell?

Paul lists idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ and complaining as warnings (vv. 7-10). Which of these feels most familiar in our world today? Which is easiest to brush off, like "do not complain" (v. 10)?
Verse 12 says, "the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall." When have you felt sure of yourself and then been caught off guard?
Verse 13 says, "He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear." Where does that feel true in your life, and where is it hard to believe? There is no wrong answer here.
Paul says, "flee from idolatry" (v. 14) and that you cannot share the Lord's table and a table of demons too (v. 21). What might be a modern table that pulls at our loyalty?

Paul calls the bread and cup "a participation in the blood of Christ" (v. 16), and Christians understand that differently, from Christ truly present in the bread and wine to a spiritual or symbolic sharing. Whatever your view, what does verse 17 say about how we should treat one another, since "we who are many are one body"?

Paul says "not everything is beneficial" and that no one should seek "his own good, but the good of others" (vv. 23, 24). Can you think of something that is fine for one person but unhelpful for another?
Verse 31 says, "whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God." What is one ordinary part of your week that you could do with that in mind?
10.life: This week, pick one area of freedom in your life, such as what you watch, buy, eat or say, and ask whether it helps the people around you. Change one small thing if it doesn't, and thank God if it does.
10.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful and provides a way through every temptation. Ask for humility to know our weak spots and for love that puts others first.
10.tip: The stories of people dying in the desert can sound harsh and leave some people anxious. Remind the group that Paul writes to believers as a loving warning, and that verse 13 sits right beside it as a promise of God's faithfulness. Keep the tone steady and encourage honest answers.

11.open: Tell us about a meal, a holiday or a potluck where someone was left out or went without. How did it feel, or what did you notice?
questions: Paul begins with "You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ" (v. 1). Who has shown you what following Jesus looks like, and what did you learn from watching them?
Paul takes it for granted that both men and women pray and prophesy in worship (vv. 4, 5). What does that tell you about how he saw the place of women in the church?

Verses 3 to 16 touch on head coverings, hair, creation and angels, and Christians read them differently. Some keep the covering as a lasting practice, many treat it as a local custom, and others see the whole passage as cultural. Where do you land, and what makes you unsure?
Verse 11 says, "In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman." How does this verse shape the way you read what comes before it?

In verse 21 "one remains hungry, another gets drunk." What would it have felt like to be one of the people who arrived late with little to bring? What does Paul's anger on their behalf tell you about God?
Paul says Jesus took the bread and cup and said, "do this in remembrance of Me" (vv. 24, 25). When you share communion, what do you find yourself remembering, or what do you find hard to feel?
Verse 26 says that when we eat this bread and drink this cup, "you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes." What does that say about what communion is for, beyond a quiet personal moment?

Paul tells each person to "examine himself" (v. 28) and later to "wait for one another" (v. 33). How can we look honestly at ourselves without sinking into guilt, and who might we need to wait for or make room for?
11.life: Look for one person in a group you belong to, at church, work or family gatherings, who is easily overlooked. This week, make room for them: save them a seat, wait for them, or share what you have.
11.prayer: Thank Jesus for giving himself for us, and ask him to show you where your gatherings leave someone out. Pray for the grace to examine yourselves honestly and to welcome one another.
11.tip: Verses 3 to 16 can take over the whole evening, and so can the argument over what happens in the bread and cup. Say once that sincere Christians disagree on both, give the head covering passage one question, and move on. Also be gentle with verses 27 to 30. Paul is speaking about one church's mistreatment of the poor, so do not let anyone take it to mean that their illness or a loved one's death was a punishment.

12.open: Think of a team, band, family or crew you have been part of. What part did you play, formally or informally?
questions: Paul says that no one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit (v. 3). What does it mean to you that simply trusting Jesus is a sign of God at work in a person?
Paul writes, "There are different gifts, but the same Spirit" (v. 4). Why do you think a church can so easily turn differences in ability into a ranking?
Verse 7 says each person's gift is given "for the common good." Think of a time someone used a gift or skill to help you. What did it look like, and how did it affect you?
Verse 11 says the Spirit gives gifts "as He determines." How does it change the way you see your own abilities, and other people's, to think of them as given rather than earned?

Paul pictures a foot saying, "Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body" (v. 15). When have you felt like you did not belong because you were not like the others? If you can't think of a time, what do you imagine that feels like for someone else?
Verse 22 says the parts that "seem to be weaker are indispensable." Who in your church or community might be easy to overlook, and what would it look like to honor them?

Verse 26 says, "If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it." Which is harder for you right now: sharing someone's pain or celebrating their success? Why?
Christians differ on whether gifts like tongues, prophecy and healing still happen today. How can our group listen to each other well on this, and what do we all agree on from this chapter?
12.life: Ask one person in your church or group what they think you are good at, and ask what you could do to serve others with it. Then find one person whose contribution often goes unnoticed and thank them in a specific way.
12.prayer: Thank God for making you part of one body, just as you are. Ask him to show each person in the group where they belong, and to help you care for one another in pain and in joy.
12.tip: Verses 8 to 10 and 28 to 30 can pull the group into a debate about tongues and healing. Say once, fairly, that Christians disagree, then bring people back to the main point: every member is needed and every gift is for others. Also watch for quiet people who think they have no gift. Gently invite them to name something others have received from them.

13.open: Think of someone who made you feel truly cared for. What did they do that made the difference?
questions: Paul says that without love, even speaking "in the tongues of men and of angels" makes him "only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal" (v. 1). Why do you think he chose that picture? What does it say about impressive things done without love?

Verses 2 and 3 list big things: knowing all mysteries, faith that moves mountains, giving away everything. Yet without love Paul says "I am nothing" (v. 2). What do you think Paul wants the Corinthians to hear, since they were proud of their gifts?
Read verses 4 to 7 slowly. Which line describes someone who has loved you well? Which one is hardest for you to live out right now?
Verse 5 says love "keeps no account of wrongs," and verse 6 says it "rejoices in the truth." How can love forgive freely and still be honest about what is wrong?
Verse 8 says "Love never fails," while prophecies, tongues and knowledge will pass away. Why might Paul say the gifts the Corinthians prized are temporary while love lasts?

Verse 12 says "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face." What questions about God or life are still blurry for you? How does it feel to hear that nobody sees fully yet?
Verse 13 says faith, hope and love remain, and "the greatest of these is love." Which of the three feels strongest in you at the moment, and which feels weakest?
Verses 4 to 7 describe love by what it does, not by how it feels. How might that change the way we think about loving people we find hard to like?
13.life: Pick one person you will see this week. Choose one line from verses 4 to 7, such as being patient or not keeping account of wrongs, and practice it with that person on purpose.
13.prayer: Ask God to teach the group to love in ways that are real and not just impressive. Pray for one relationship where patience or kindness is needed.
13.tip: Verses 4 to 7 are often read at weddings, so some people hear them as sweet and soft. Remind the group that Paul wrote them to a divided, boastful church, and invite people to hear them as a challenge to everyday behavior. Also, if someone asks when "the perfect" comes (v. 10), say briefly that most read it as Christ's return, some read it differently, and bring the group back to love.

14.open: Tell about a time you were in a room where everyone else seemed to know the language, the rules or the inside jokes, and you didn't. How did it feel?
questions: Paul begins, "Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts" (v. 1). Why do you think he puts love first? What changes if we reverse the order?

Paul says the one who prophesies "edifies the church" while the one who speaks in a tongue "edifies himself" (v. 4). In your own words, what is Paul asking this church to care about most when they meet?

Paul compares unclear speech to a flute, a harp and a trumpet that gives a "muffled call" (vv. 7-8). Where do we make church life confusing for newcomers, with jargon, habits or things everyone just assumes?

Paul says he would rather speak "five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue" (v. 19). When has a short, plain word from someone helped you more than something long or impressive?
Verses 24 and 25 describe an outsider who comes in and says, "God is truly among you!" What would help a visitor sense that in our group or church?

Verse 26 says, "All of these must be done to build up the church." What do you bring to a gathering, and how could it serve others and not just yourself? If you aren't sure you bring anything, say so honestly. That is a fair answer here.
Christians disagree about what tongues were and whether these gifts continue today. How can people who see this differently still worship and learn together?

Paul ends with "be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner" (vv. 39-40). How do you hold together freedom and order in your own faith?
14.life: This week, look at one thing you do in a group, whether at church, work or home, through the eyes of a newcomer. Change one thing so someone else can understand it or join in more easily.
14.prayer: Ask God to teach each of you to love others first and to use whatever you have to build them up. Pray for anyone in the group who feels like an outsider.
14.tip: Verses 34 and 35 on women and silence will likely come up, and sincere Christians read them differently. Some see a lasting limit on women speaking or teaching in worship. Others see a local rule about disruptive questions. Say that plainly, note that chapter 11 has women praying and prophesying aloud, and keep the group on Paul's main concern, which is building each other up. Don't try to settle it tonight.

15.open: What is something you have planted or tried to grow, and how did it turn out?
questions: Paul passed on "as of first importance" that Christ died, was buried and was raised (v. 3). Why might he put these first? If someone asked what is of first importance in your faith, what would you say?

Paul lists people who saw the risen Jesus, including "more than five hundred brothers at once" (v. 6). Why name witnesses who could still be asked? How does that kind of evidence land with you: helpful, not enough, or beside the point?

Paul had persecuted the church, yet he says, "by the grace of God I am what I am" (v. 10). How does his past shape the way he talks about himself? Where do you need grace to have the last word about who you are?

Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, "our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith" (v. 14). Why is he so blunt? Be honest: how real does the resurrection feel to you right now, and what questions do you carry about it?

Paul calls Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (v. 20). The first part of a harvest promises the rest will follow. What does it change to think of Jesus as the first and not the only one?

Paul compares burial to planting a seed (vv. 36-42). Christians differ on whether the raised body is this same body transformed or a new kind of body that keeps the person. What hopes or worries come up for you when you picture rising?
Paul asks, "Where, O Death, is your sting?" (v. 55). Where has death or loss touched your life? What would it look like to hold that loss next to this hope?
Paul says if the dead are not raised, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (v. 32). Have you seen what people believe about death shape how they live, in yourself or in others?
15.life: Think of someone who has lost a loved one. This week, send them a short note or message saying you are thinking of them, and if it fits, share one line of hope from this chapter.
15.prayer: Thank God that "thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 57) is true. Ask him to steady anyone in the group who is grieving or doubting, and to make you steady in your work for him.
15.tip: Verse 29 about baptism for the dead will probably come up, and nobody knows for sure what it meant. Say so in one line, note that Christians read it differently, and bring the group back to Paul's main point: the resurrection of Christ and what it promises.

16.open: Think of a time you helped plan a trip, a meal or a project for a group. What job did you end up with?
questions: Paul asks each person to "set aside a portion of his income" on the first day of every week (v. 2). What does it say about giving that he asks for a steady habit and not a one-time rush?

The money was for poor believers in Jerusalem, and the Corinthians would pick their own trusted people to carry it (v. 3). Why might it matter that the gift was handled openly, and where do we need that kind of openness today?
Paul says "a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me" (v. 9). How can opposition and opportunity show up together? Have you seen that in your own life?

Paul tells the church, "No one, then, should treat him with contempt" about Timothy (v. 11). Who in your church or community can be overlooked or talked down to, and how could we make them feel welcome?
Paul gives short commands in verses 13 and 14: "Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith." and "Do everything in love." Which one is hardest for you this season, and why?

Stephanas and his household "devoted themselves to the service of the saints" (v. 15), and Paul asks the church to appreciate people like them. Who serves quietly in your life, and how could you thank them this week?

Paul ends a letter that corrected the church sharply with "My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus" (v. 24). When someone has been honest with you about a problem, what helps you believe they still care about you?

Paul says "If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse," and then prays "Come, O Lord!" (v. 22). Whether you feel sure, unsure or somewhere in between, what does it stir up in you to hear that?
16.life: Pick one person who serves quietly in your church, family or neighborhood. This week, thank them in a note or in person, and be specific about what they do. If you can, also set aside a small, regular amount to give to someone in need.
16.prayer: Ask God for steady faith and for love in everything you do. Thank him for the people who serve without fanfare, and pray for anyone in the group who feels tired or opposed right now.
16.tip: Verse 22 sounds harsh, and people may stumble over the word "curse." Don't rush past it or soften it. Point out that it comes right before "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you" (v. 23), and let a doubting person say honestly how it lands. Also be aware that verse 13 says "Be men of courage," but the call to courage and strength is for everyone in the group.
